newsitem.title: USA: Louisana Democrat winner a rarity in Deep South.
newsitem.headline: Louisana Democrat winner a rarity in Deep South.

text.p: Louisiana's Democratic entry in the November sweepstakes for the Senate is a rarity in the Deep South, a 40-year-old, pro-choice Catholic.
Although Mary Landrieu had led the polls throughout the campaign for retiring Democrat J. Bennett Johnston's seat, she barely squeaked into a runoff slot in Saturday's primary election.

The come-from-behind Republican who placed first Saturday in the multi-party primary is state Representative Woody Jenkins, a conservative anti-abortion leader who had been running third or fourth in the polls until the last week of the campaign.

Landrieu, who served two terms in the House starting at age 25, narrowly lost a spot on the general election ballot in last fall's governor's race. She has also served two terms as state treasurer, one of only a handful of women to hold state-wide elective office in Louisiana and across the Deep South.
Her father was one of New Orleans' most popular two-term mayors, Moon Landrieu, now a judge, who also served as President Jimmy Carter's secretary of housing and urban development.
Landrieu is married to lawyer Frank Snellings, and they have a 4-year-old son, Conner.
Landrieu and Jenkins both call themselves middle-of-the road candidates, but the differences between the two are many and unambiguous.

She opposes reducing the budget and regulatory powers of the Environmental Protection Agency and opening part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil exploration and drilling. He supports both measures.

He would repeal the ban on certain assault weapons; she would not. Both support the death penalty, limiting federal appeals by death-row inmates, and a constitutional amendment requiring a balanced federal budget, but she supports affirmative action, which he vows to end.
Jenkins surprise first-place finish suggests Landrieu has an uphill fight.

A major political spat with Representative Cleo Fields, who along with Landrieu was a loser in the 1995 governor's race, has continued for a year, with Fields -- who carries a lot of weight in black communities -- endorsing her Democratic rival in the senatorial primary.

It is not clear if he will now endorse Landrieu or just stay out of the race. But she will need a significant number of black votes to pull off a November victory, particularly if Republican Mike Foster, a very popular governor, actively stumps for Jenkins.
